questions.question: Dicuss on Oxidation, Reduction and Redox Potential?
questions.solution_html:
• Oxidation, Reduction and Redox Potential –
  • Oxidation: It is the process in which an atom, ion, or molecule loses electrons. This loss of electrons
  • increases the oxidation state of the substance. In simple terms, oxidation is the "loss of electrons".
  • Eg: - Fe→Fe2++2e−(Definition - (1 mark), Example ½ mark)
  • Reduction: It is the process in which an atom, ion, or molecule gains electron. This gain of electrons
  • decreases the oxidation state of the substance. In simple terms, reduction is the "gain of electrons".
  • Eg: -Cu2++2e− → Cu(Definition - (1 mark), Example ½ mark)
  • Redox Potential: - The oxidation-reduction potential or, simply, redox potential, is a quantitative
  • measure of the tendency of a redox pair to lose or gain electrons. The redox pairs are assigned specific
  • standard redox potential (E0 volts) at pH 7.0 and 25°C. (Definition - (2 marks))

questions.question: Discuss on passive transport?
questions.solution_html:
• Passive Transport –
  • Definition - (2 marks)
  • Types – (3 marks) for each type
  •  No energy required; occurs down the concentration gradient (high to low concentration).
  •  Naturally occurring process; cell does not use energy.
  •  Main types: Simple diffusion, Facilitated diffusion, and Osmosis.
  • Simple Diffusion
  •  Random movement of particles from high to low concentration.
  •  Continues until equilibrium (even distribution) is reached.
  • Facilitated Diffusion
  •  Movement of ions or polar molecules with the help of membrane proteins.
  •  Uses transmembrane integral proteins to allow passage.
  •  No energy used; relies on concentration gradient.
  •  Proteins protect molecules from the membrane's hydrophobic core.
  • Osmosis
  •  Diffusion of water through a semi-permeable membrane.
  •  Water moves from higher water concentration to lower water concentration.
  •  Movement is inversely related to solute concentration.
questions.final_answer:  Movement is inversely related to solute concentration

questions.question: Explain the stages of oxidation in food?
questions.solution_html:
• Stages of Oxidation –
  • Stages – (2 mark)

  •  Digestion in the gastrointestinal tract breaks macromolecules into small units.
  •  Example: Proteins → Amino acids.
  • • Second Stage – Secondary / Intermediary Metabolism
  •  Absorbed products are further catabolised and oxidised to CO₂..
  •  Occurs mainly in mitochondria via the citric acid cycle.
  •  Generates reducing equivalents: NADH and FADH₂..
  • • Third Stage – Tertiary Metabolism / Cellular Respiration
  •  NADH and FADH₂. enter the electron transport chain (ETC).
  •  Energy is released and used for body’s synthetic activities.
  •  Phototrophs use light energy (e.g., plants); chemotrophs use energy from fuel oxidation.
questions.final_answer:  Phototrophs use light energy (e.g., plants); chemotrophs use energy from fuel oxidation

questions.question: Which type of carrier protein moves one molecule in one direction? / a). Symport b). Antiport c). Uniport d). Bipolar
questions.solution_html:
• Uniport
  • Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) ( (1mark))
  •  Accepts electrons from NADH
  •  Transfers them to the next carrier
  •  Pumps protons (H⁺) into the intermembrane space
  • Single-stranded molecule
  •  RNA is usually single-stranded, unlike DNA.
  • Genetic (Linkage) Mapping ((2 marks))
  •  Based on recombination frequency during meiosis
  •  Distance is measured in centimorgans (cM)
  •  The more recombination, the farther apart the genes
  •  Does not give exact physical distance, only relative positions
  • Substrate-Level Phosphorylation ((4 marks))
  • Definition
  • Direct formation of ATP by transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy substrate to
  • ADP.
  • Sites
  •  Cytoplasm → during glycolysis
  •  Mitochondrial matrix → during Krebs cycle
  • Examples
  •  1,3-bisphosphoglycerate → 3-phosphoglycerate
  •  Phosphoenolpyruvate → Pyruvate
  • Features
  •  Does not require oxygen, hence occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions
  •  Produces a small amount of ATP
  •  Provides rapid and immediate energy to the cell
  •  Important in tissues with low oxygen supply and in cells lacking mitochondria
  • Point mutations
  • A change occurs in a single base of DNA, which may involve substitution, insertion, or
  • deletion, potentially altering gene function.
  • Direct Repair
  • This mechanism directly reverses DNA damage without removing the base, such as the
  • photoreactivation of thymine dimers.
  • Transcription (in nucleus) ((3 marks))
  • Definition
  • Synthesis of RNA from DNA using RNA polymerase.
  • Steps of Transcription
  • a. Initiation
  •  RNA polymerase binds to the promoter region of DNA
  •  DNA unwinds to expose the template strand
  • b. Elongation
  •  RNA polymerase moves along the DNA template (3′ → 5′)
  •  Synthesizes pre-mRNA in 5′ → 3′ direction
  •  Complementary base pairing occurs (A–U, G–C)
  • c. Termination
  •  RNA polymerase reaches the termination signal
  •  Pre-mRNA is released
  • Post-Transcriptional Modifications (in nucleus) ((2 marks))
  • The primary transcript (pre-mRNA / hnRNA) is processed into mature mRNA
  • 5′ Capping
  •  Addition of 7-methyl guanosine cap
  •  Protects mRNA and helps ribosome binding
  • Folding
  •  Protein folds into its 3D structure (often with chaperones)

  • Oxidative Phosphorylation ((4 marks))
  • Definition
  • ATP synthesis using energy released from electron transfer in the electron transport chain
  • (ETC).
  • Site
  •  Inner mitochondrial membrane
  • Process
  •  Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ pass through a series of carriers in the ETC
  •  Energy released during electron transfer is used to pump protons (H⁺) into the
  • intermembrane space
  •  This creates an electrochemical proton gradient (proton motive force)
  •  Protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, driving the formation of ATP
  • from ADP and Pi
  •  This mechanism is explained by the chemiosmotic theory
  • Role of Oxygen
  •  Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor
  •  It combines with electrons and protons to form water
  •  This prevents the accumulation of electrons and allows the chain to continue
  • functioning
  • Features
  •  Produces the maximum amount of ATP (~28–32 ATP per glucose)
  •  Requires oxygen, hence it is an aerobic process
  •  Highly efficient and supplies most of the energy required for cellular activities
  •  Occurs only in cells with functional mitochondria
  • UV-induced damage
  • Ultraviolet radiation causes the formation of thymine dimers, which distort the DNA helix
  • and interfere with replication.
  • Base Excision Repair (BER)
  • Damaged bases are recognized, removed, and replaced with the correct bases by specific
  • enzymes.
  • 3′ Poly-A Tail
  •  Addition of adenine nucleotides
  •  Increases stability of mRNA
  • Translation (in cytoplasm) ((3 marks))
  • Definition
  • Synthesis of protein from mRNA on ribosomes.
  • Steps of Translation
  • a. Initiation
  •  Small ribosomal subunit binds to mRNA
  •  Recognizes start codon (AUG)
  •  Initiator tRNA carrying methionine binds
  •  Large subunit joins to form complete ribosome
  • b. Elongation
  •  tRNA brings specific amino acids to ribosome
  •  Codon–anticodon pairing ensures correct sequence
  •  Peptide bonds form between amino acids
  •  Ribosome moves along mRNA (translocation)
  • c. Termination
  •  Ribosome reaches a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA)
  •  Release factors bind
  •  Polypeptide chain is released
  • Post-Translational Modifications ((1 mark))
  • After translation, the protein becomes functional through modifications
  • Chemical modifications
  •  Phosphorylation, glycosylation, acetylation, etc.

questions.question: List down the factors affecting diffusion rate.
questions.solution_html:
• List down the factors affecting diffusion rate. (Any 5 points (1 mark) each)
  •  Temperature
  • Higher temperature → increases molecular energy and movement → faster
  • diffusion
  • Lower temperature → decreases molecular energy → slower diffusion
  •  Solubility
  • Nonpolar/lipid-soluble substances diffuse faster than polar substances
  •  Concentration Gradient
  • Greater concentration difference → faster diffusion
  •  Mass of Molecules
  • Heavier molecules → move slowly → slower diffusion
  • Lighter molecules → move faster → faster diffusion
  •  Density of Solvent
  • Higher density → slower diffusion (more resistance to movement)
  • Lower density → faster diffusion
  •  Surface Area / Membrane Thickness
  • Increased surface area → faster diffusion
  • Thicker membrane → slower diffusion
  •  Distance Travelled
  • Greater distance → slower diffusion
  • Shorter distance → faster diffusion

questions.question: Explain facilitated diffusion.
questions.solution_html:
•  Facilitated diffusion is a type of passive transport (also called facilitated
  • transport).
  •  Substances move across the plasma membrane with the help of membrane
  • proteins (transmembrane integral proteins).
  •  Movement occurs along the concentration gradient (high → low concentration).
  •  No cellular energy (ATP) is required.
  •  Mainly involves ions and polar molecules that cannot pass through the
  • hydrophobic lipid bilayer.
  •  Membrane proteins protect these substances from repulsion by the membrane.
  •  Substances first bind to specific protein or glycoprotein receptors on the outer
  • surface.
  •  Then they are transferred to integral proteins for transport across the membrane.
  •  Types of transport proteins involved
  • Channel proteins: form pores (often made of β-pleated sheets) for passage
  • Carrier proteins: bind to substances and assist their movement across the
  • membrane

questions.question: List down the factors affecting diffusion rate.
questions.solution_html:
• List down the factors affecting diffusion rate. (Any 5 points (1 mark) each)
  •  Temperature
  • Higher temperature → increases molecular energy and movement → faster
  • diffusion
  • Lower temperature → decreases molecular energy → slower diffusion
  •  Solubility
  • Nonpolar/lipid-soluble substances diffuse faster than polar substances
  •  Concentration Gradient
  • Greater concentration difference → faster diffusion
  •  Mass of Molecules
  • Heavier molecules → move slowly → slower diffusion
  • Lighter molecules → move faster → faster diffusion
  •  Density of Solvent
  • Higher density → slower diffusion (more resistance to movement)
  • Lower density → faster diffusion
  •  Surface Area / Membrane Thickness
  • Increased surface area → faster diffusion
  • Thicker membrane → slower diffusion
  •  Distance Travelled
  • Greater distance → slower diffusion
  • Shorter distance → faster diffusion
